# Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN): expert reading notes

Numbers only where read in the cited source (locator in brackets). [consensus] = several groups agree;
[disputed] = sources disagree. hBN is a wide-gap insulator: no Kohn anomaly, no double resonance, so its
Raman spectrum is far poorer in information than graphene's; most of what it tells is strain, isotope
content, thickness via intensity, and crystal quality via width.

## Signature
- One strong high-frequency line, the in-plane E2g (often called "G band" by analogy with graphene), at about
  1366 cm-1 in bulk crystals (Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465; arXiv 1008.2868, p.3). Bulk value
  1366.6 +- 0.2 cm-1 over 6 crystals (Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059; arXiv 2008.01656, p.7).
  [consensus]
- Bulk width: HWHM about 9 cm-1 (Gorbachev 2011, p.4); FWHM about 9 cm-1 for bulk flakes in heterostructures
  (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387; doi 10.1038/s41467-018-07558-3, p.6, via Lit-RAG).
- Low-frequency interlayer shear E2g near 50 cm-1 in bulk; needs a low-frequency setup (Janzen et al. 2023,
  arXiv 2306.13358, p.7).
- Monolayer signal is weak: about 50 times smaller than graphene G under the same conditions (Gorbachev
  2011, p.3). Long integration and Si second-order background become relevant.

## Thickness and stacking
- Integrated E2g intensity is proportional to N for the first several layers on a given substrate; once
  calibrated, this distinguishes 1, 2 and more layers (Gorbachev 2011, p.4, Fig. 4a inset). [consensus]
- Position as a layer test [disputed]:
  - Gorbachev 2011 (pp.1, 4, Fig. 4b): 1L upshifted typically 2 to 4 cm-1 (sample dependent, +- 2 cm-1),
    2L usually downshifted 1 to 2 cm-1; attributed to shorter B-N bond plus random strain.
  - Cai 2017 (pp.7-8, Fig. 1): substrate-bound 1L 1369.6 +- 0.6, 2L 1369.0 +- 0.5, 3L 1367.5 +- 0.2 cm-1;
    suspended 1L to 3L 1367.0 to 1367.3 cm-1, close to bulk. DFT finds the intrinsic E2g nearly N-independent.
    Conclusion: shifts in thin hBN come mainly from substrate strain, not thickness.
  - Practical reading: a 1 to 4 cm-1 upshift is consistent with 1L but not proof; use intensity steps,
    optical contrast or AFM.
- Optical contrast of 1L on SiO2 is small (under 1.5 % white light) and changes sign near 530 nm; about
  2.5 % per layer on about 80 nm SiO2 (Gorbachev 2011, pp.1-3). Monolayers can look like bilayers without
  annealing (same, p.3).

## Strain and doping
- Strain dominates thin-hBN shifts; it may vary within the laser spot as the flake follows substrate
  roughness, which also broadens the line (Gorbachev 2011, p.4). 1L HWHM 10 to 12 cm-1 vs about 9 bulk.
- Annealing at 400 C on SiO2/Si increased roughness and upshifted 1L by 3.0 +- 0.7 cm-1 (2L 2.7, 3L 2.2);
  bulk unchanged (Cai 2017, pp.13-16, Fig. 4). Thermal-expansion mismatch with SiO2 is the proposed cause.
- Doping: monolayer BN is not subject to surface doping (insulator), so doping is not a usual explanation
  of shifts (Cai 2017, p.7, citing earlier work).

## Defects and quality
- Width is the main quality indicator, but isotope disorder sets a floor: natural boron (about 20 % 10B,
  80 % 11B) gives FWHM about 7.5 to 8 cm-1; monoisotopic crystals about 3 to 4 cm-1 (Janzen 2023, pp.3, 7).
  A natural-abundance crystal cannot be narrower than this floor regardless of quality. [consensus]
- Isotope shifts are large: about 1393 cm-1 for h10B14N, 1357 for h11BN, down to about 1335 cm-1 for h11B15N
  (Janzen 2023, pp.3, 7, Fig. 4b). A line far from 1366 may be isotope engineering, not strain.
- No defect-activated band analogous to graphene D is established for hBN in the sources read here; I do
  not have a sourced Raman defect metric beyond width and position. [not verified]

## Temperature and heating
- E2g softens on heating: a 1L line moved to 1367.7 cm-1 at 75 C and 1366.4 cm-1 at 100 C (Cai 2017, p.7).
  Heating therefore cannot explain upshifts of thin hBN on SiO2.
- Example measurement practice: power kept below 300 uW at 0.5 NA to avoid heating (Janzen 2023, p.7).
  hBN absorbs little visible light, so heating is usually a lesser concern than for graphene. [inference]

## Excitation wavelength
- hBN E2g does not disperse with laser energy (no double resonance or Kohn anomaly), unlike graphene D
  (Purdie 2018, p.6). Changing the laser separates an hBN line from a graphene D peak.
- Wide gap: visible excitation is far from resonance; UV benefits wide-gap layered materials (Ferrari and Basko
  2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, p.12). [qualitative]

## Polarization and substrate
- In-plane E2g of a hexagonal crystal gives no in-plane angular contrast in parallel or crossed
  backscattering. [inference from symmetry, not from a source read here]
- In heterostructures the hBN line is the sum of top and bottom flakes (Purdie 2018, p.6); thickness
  assignments from intensity need each flake measured separately.
- hBN encapsulation narrows graphene 2D (16 to 20 vs above 22 cm-1 on SiO2) and the hBN line serves to map
  encapsulated areas (Neumann et al. 2015, Nat. Commun. 6, 8429; arXiv 1406.7771, p.2, Fig. 1e,h).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- hBN E2g at about 1366 cm-1 overlaps graphene D (about 1350 at 514 nm): in encapsulated graphene a peak near
  1360 is not automatically defects; check with a second laser (Purdie 2018, p.6).
- Weak 1L signal: confirm the line is above the Si second-order background and noise.
- Peak position differences of 1 to 3 cm-1 are within strain and calibration scatter; never assign layer
  number from position alone (Gorbachev 2011; Cai 2017).
- Width comparisons only between crystals of the same isotope composition.

## What to ask
- Bulk source (HPHT, flux-grown, CVD), isotope composition; exfoliated, CVD or polymer-transferred.
- Supported or suspended; annealed or not; substrate and oxide thickness.
- Laser, power, resolution (hBN widths of 3 to 9 cm-1 are close to many instruments' resolution).
- Whether low-frequency (shear mode) data exist.

## Reference figures
- Gorbachev 2011, arXiv 1008.2868, Fig. 4: 1L to 3L spectra, intensity vs N, position vs N with sample scatter.
- Cai 2017, arXiv 2008.01656, Fig. 1 and Fig. 4: supported vs suspended positions; upshift after annealing.
- Janzen 2023, arXiv 2306.13358, Fig. 4: E2g position and width for four isotope combinations.

# Artifacts and red flags in Raman spectra of 2D materials

Each entry: what it looks like, how to tell it from a real band, what to do. Sources in brackets.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

## Cosmic-ray spikes
- One to three pixels wide, far narrower than any phonon line at the instrument resolution, present in one
  acquisition only. Real lines have the instrument's minimum width and repeat across accumulations or angles.
- Remove before fitting (modified z-score on the first difference: Whitaker and Hayes, Chemom. Intell. Lab. Syst.
  179, 82, 2018). In an angle series, replace spike pixels from the most similar frame (Barton and Hennelly, Appl.
  Spectrosc. 73, 893, 2019). List them under artifacts, never under peaks.

## Silicon substrate
- First-order Si line near 520.7 cm-1 (a widely used calibration convention; check the offset of the fitted
  position and flag a calibration problem when it exceeds about 1 cm-1; 520 to 520.9 is reported in practice, Lee
  et al. 2010 and Castellanos-Gomez et al. 2014). Second-order Si features near 950 and 980 cm-1 (Gillet et al.
  2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1) and a 2TA band computed near 300 cm-1 (same paper, DFPT) can be mistaken for
  sample modes. Brillouin scattering from Si gives a line near
  4.5 cm-1 in ultra-low-frequency setups (Zhang et al., PRB 87, 115413, 2013).
- Assign these as 'Si substrate'. A strong Si line with weak sample bands suggests a thin flake.

## Calibration
- First-order wavelength calibration errors of 5 to 7 cm-1 have been reported (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024,
  2012). Shifts of 1 to 3 cm-1 (layer number, strain, doping) are only meaningful after a calibration check.

## Background
- Broad fluorescence or photoluminescence slopes; remove with an asymmetric least-squares baseline (arPLS or
  asPLS). For broad bands (disordered carbon D and G, amorphous phases) a global baseline can eat real signal: fit
  a local linear background together with the peaks. A Breit-Wigner-Fano line shape can absorb a background slope;
  compare line shapes by BIC.

## Low-wavenumber cutoff
- Notch and edge filters block the region near the laser line (Bragg notch filters reach about 5 to 10 cm-1,
  Zhang et al. 2013). A missing shear or breathing mode below the cutoff is not evidence of absence.

## Plasma lines
- Laser plasma lines have a fixed absolute wavelength, so their Raman shift changes when the laser changes; they
  are very narrow and do not belong to the sample. Suspect them when a narrow line has no assignment.

## Laser heating
- Phonon lines soften and broaden with temperature. Graphene G shifts about -0.016 cm-1/K (Calizo et al., Nano
  Lett. 7, 2645, 2007); 1L WS2 about -0.0093 (E) and -0.0122 (A1g) cm-1/K (Huang et al., Sci. Rep. 2016);
  few-layer MoS2 about -0.013 and -0.012 cm-1/K (Sahoo et al., arXiv 1302.5865). A power series is the test.

## Substrate interference
- On SiO2/Si, absolute intensities and intensity ratios depend on oxide thickness and laser wavelength: graphene
  I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al., PRB 80, 125422, 2009).
  Never read layer number from absolute intensity or from I(2D)/I(G) without the substrate stack.

## Resonance
- Near an excitonic resonance, second-order bands can exceed first-order ones. WS2 at 514 to 532 nm: 2LA(M) lies
  about 4 cm-1 below E2g and overlaps it (Berkdemir et al., Sci. Rep. 3, 1755, 2013; Mitioglu et al., PRB 89,
  245442, 2014). Fit both or the E2g position and layer count are wrong.

## Saturation and clipping
- A flat-topped peak or values at the detector maximum: the peak shape and intensity are wrong; ask for a shorter
  exposure.

input.summary: Flake 2 is a thin hBN flake, and it could be a monolayer, but Raman alone cannot show that it is. Its E2g line is about 10x weaker than flake 1's and sits 2.85 ± 0.25 cm-1 higher (1368.8–1369.0 cm-1), with a 3–4 cm-1 larger FWHM. All of that fits a 1L flake, but it fits a 2L flake on SiO2 equally well. The extra bands at 950/980 cm-1 are Si second-order lines, not hBN. Confirming N=1 needs AFM, or a calibrated intensity ladder measured on the same substrate and spectrometer. I would not call it a monolayer in print on this evidence.

observations.finding: Both flakes are hBN. Each shows the in-plane E2g line near 1366–1369 cm-1 and nothing else belonging to the sample in 450–1650 cm-1. No carbon D/G is present in flake 2.
observations.evidence: Flake 1 E2g: 1366.0–1366.2 cm-1 (Lorentzian, ±0.08), FWHM 15.5 (ALS baseline) or 18.0 (local linear background), peak height about 3060 counts, SNR about 72. Flake 2 E2g: 1368.8–1369.0 cm-1 (±0.24), FWHM 18.8 ± 0.8 (ALS) or 21.8 ± 0.8 (local linear), height about 250 counts. The region 1500–1640 is flat in flake 2 (slope 0.16 counts/cm-1, noise about 19), so no G band near 1580.
observations.source: Bulk E2g about 1366 cm-1: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465 (arXiv 1008.2868, p.3); Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656, p.7)

observations.finding: The E2g line of flake 2 is upshifted by about +2.9 cm-1 relative to flake 1. This is larger than the calibration scatter, so it is probably real.
observations.evidence: Shift 2.85 ± 0.25 cm-1 (fit error only) from rl_series. The Si 520 line sits at 520.93 in flake 1 and 520.90 in flake 2, offset +0.2 cm-1 in both, so calibration cancels. Allowing a few tenths of a cm-1 of extra calibration scatter, the shift is still more than 5 sigma. Flake 1 at 1366.0–1366.2 matches the bulk value of 1366.6 ± 0.2.

observations.finding: The position is compatible with 1L, but it cannot tell 1L from 2L, and strain from the substrate and from transfer dominates it. The sources are also in disagreement on whether position tracks layer number at all.

structured_output.summary: Flake 2 is a thin hBN flake, and it could be a monolayer, but Raman alone cannot show that it is. Its E2g line is about 10x weaker than flake 1's and sits 2.85 ± 0.25 cm-1 higher (1368.8–1369.0 cm-1), with a 3–4 cm-1 larger FWHM. All of that fits a 1L flake, but it fits a 2L flake on SiO2 equally well. The extra bands at 950/980 cm-1 are Si second-order lines, not hBN. Confirming N=1 needs AFM, or a calibrated intensity ladder measured on the same substrate and spectrometer. I would not call it a monolayer in print on this evidence.

observations.finding: Both flakes are hBN. Each shows the in-plane E2g line near 1366–1369 cm-1 and nothing else belonging to the sample in 450–1650 cm-1. No carbon D/G is present in flake 2.
observations.evidence: Flake 1 E2g: 1366.0–1366.2 cm-1 (Lorentzian, ±0.08), FWHM 15.5 (ALS baseline) or 18.0 (local linear background), peak height about 3060 counts, SNR about 72. Flake 2 E2g: 1368.8–1369.0 cm-1 (±0.24), FWHM 18.8 ± 0.8 (ALS) or 21.8 ± 0.8 (local linear), height about 250 counts. The region 1500–1640 is flat in flake 2 (slope 0.16 counts/cm-1, noise about 19), so no G band near 1580.
observations.source: Bulk E2g about 1366 cm-1: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465 (arXiv 1008.2868, p.3); Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059 (arXiv 2008.01656, p.7)

observations.finding: The E2g line of flake 2 is upshifted by about +2.9 cm-1 relative to flake 1. This is larger than the calibration scatter, so it is probably real.
observations.evidence: Shift 2.85 ± 0.25 cm-1 (fit error only) from rl_series. The Si 520 line sits at 520.93 in flake 1 and 520.90 in flake 2, offset +0.2 cm-1 in both, so calibration cancels. Allowing a few tenths of a cm-1 of extra calibration scatter, the shift is still more than 5 sigma. Flake 1 at 1366.0–1366.2 matches the bulk value of 1366.6 ± 0.2.

observations.finding: The position is compatible with 1L, but it cannot tell 1L from 2L, and strain from the substrate and from transfer dominates it. The sources are also in disagreement on whether position tracks layer number at all.
observations.evidence: Gorbachev 2011 (pp.1, 4, Fig. 4b): 1L upshifted 2–4 cm-1 (±2), 2L usually downshifted 1–2 cm-1. Flake 2 is +2.6 to +2.9 vs bulk, which fits 1L under Gorbachev. Cai 2017 (pp.7–8, Fig. 1) reports substrate-bound 1L at 1369.6 ± 0.6 and 2L at 1369.0 ± 0.5, and 3L at 1367.5 ± 0.2. Flake 2 (1368.8–1369.0 ± 0.24) matches 2L slightly better and 1L within 1–3 sigma. Cai concludes the shifts are mainly substrate strain. Annealing alone adds +2.2 to +3.0 cm-1 (Cai Fig. 4), so the shift may reflect thermal history, not N.
observations.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465, Fig. 4b, arXiv 1008.2868; Cai et al. 2017, Nanoscale 9, 3059, Fig. 1 and Fig. 4, arXiv 2008.01656

observations.finding: Flake 2's E2g line is about 10x weaker than flake 1's. This points to a thinner flake, but it is not a layer count because flake 1's thickness is unknown.
observations.evidence: Integrated E2g area: flake 1 74.6e3 (ALS fit) or 91e3 (local fit); flake 2 7.3e3 or 9.2e3. Ratio 10.2 (ALS) or 9.9 (local). Same laser, power and integration time. If the area scales linearly with N, flake 1 is about 10x as thick as flake 2, and N2 = 1 only if flake 1 is about 10 layers (about 3.3 nm). Gorbachev 2011 (Fig. 4a inset) gives linearity for the first several layers on a given substrate.
observations.source: Gorbachev et al. 2011, Small 7, 465, Fig. 4a inset (intensity proportional to N), arXiv 1008.2868

observations.finding: The Si-normalised intensity is very different from the absolute ratio, so the two spots cannot be compared directly. The Si signal in flake 1 is about 18x weaker than in flake 2, which is odd for a flake that is transparent at 514 nm.
observations.evidence: Si 520 height: 981 counts (flake 1) vs 17993 (flake 2); area 5.3e3 vs 97.9e3. E2g/Si area: 14 (flake 1) vs 0.075 (flake 2), a factor of about 190. The absolute ratio is 10x and the Si-normalised ratio is about 190x. A 3 nm flake would not suppress Si 18x. Flake 1 is therefore either much thicker than 10 layers (interference/refraction, and consistent with its sloping 500→1200 count baseline), or it was measured with different focus or collection. If flake 1 is much thicker than 10 layers, flake 2 would be several layers, not 1L. Flake 2 gives E2g/Si 0.075 and has a flat baseline, so its Si is effectively unattenuated.

observations.finding: The bands at about 950 and 979 cm-1 in flake 2 are second-order silicon (2TO), not hBN. Their presence confirms that flake 2 is thin enough for the Si substrate to dominate the spectrum.
observations.evidence: Positions 950.4 ± 0.4 and 979.3 ± 0.4 cm-1, FWHM 19 and 17 cm-1, heights 283 and 286 counts, about 1.6 % of the Si 520 height (17993). They are absent in flake 1, where the Si 520 line is 18x weaker and the 2TO would sit below the noise (about 40 counts). The strong Si line with weak sample bands is the signature of a thin flake.
observations.source: Gillet et al. 2017, arXiv 1708.05874, Fig. 1 (Si second-order features near 950 and 980 cm-1); reference/artifacts.md

observations.finding: The weak feature at about 1474 cm-1 in the flake 2 fit is noise and should not be assigned.
observations.evidence: Height 59 ± 41 counts, FWHM 3.4 ± 5.5 cm-1 (error larger than the value), against local noise std about 19 counts. It is a 2–3 sigma excursion in a 1440–1510 window of about 90 points.

observations.finding: The width of flake 2 is slightly larger than flake 1, which is consistent with a thin strained flake but is not diagnostic.
observations.evidence: FWHM difference +3.3 (ALS) or +3.8 (local) cm-1, with a fit error of about 0.8 and a baseline-dependent systematic of about 3 cm-1 in absolute width. Gorbachev 2011 gives 1L HWHM 10–12 vs about 9 bulk, i.e. FWHM about 20–24 vs about 18. Flake 2's HWHM is 9.4–10.9 and flake 1's is 7.8–9.0. The width is baseline-dependent, so the 3 cm-1 broadening is marginal.

observations.finding: The faint optical appearance of flake 2 is consistent with a very thin flake but does not fix N.
observations.evidence: Gorbachev 2011 (pp.1–3) gives 1L contrast under 1.5 % in white light, about 2.5 % per layer on about 80 nm SiO2, and a sign change near 530 nm. Our 290 nm oxide and 514.5 nm laser are not the conditions in that study, so I did not scale the contrast.

caveats: Layer number from position is disputed. Gorbachev 2011 attributes the 1L upshift to shorter bonds plus strain; Cai 2017 attributes thin-hBN shifts mainly to substrate strain and shows the suspended 1L–3L lines are within 0.3 cm-1 of bulk. A +2.9 cm-1 shift fits 1L, 2L and an annealed or strained thicker flake.

The intensity comparison depends on the thickness of flake 1, which is unknown, and on E2g intensity staying linear in N, which only holds for the first several layers on a given substrate. Interference on 290 nm SiO2 at 514.5 nm modulates the intensity per layer, so absolute counts are not layer number.

The Si 520 intensity differs 18x between the two spots, so focus, collection or flake thickness changed between measurements. This weakens any normalisation to Si, and the absolute E2g ratio (about 10x) and the Si-normalised ratio (about 190x) point to different thickness ratios. I could not reconcile them from the data alone.

The width values depend on the baseline model: ALS gives 15.5 and 18.8, a local linear background gives 18.0 and 21.8. The literature notes also disagree on bulk width (HWHM about 9 in Gorbachev vs FWHM about 9 in Purdie 2018 and a natural-boron floor of 7.5–8 FWHM in Janzen 2023). Flake 1's FWHM of 15.5–18 is about 2x the Cai/Purdie bulk values, and the Si line FWHM (3.4–3.5) rules out instrument broadening as the main cause. Treat only the flake-to-flake difference (+3–4 cm-1) as measured and do not read absolute widths as crystal quality.

Raw intensities in flake 2 sit on a Si second-order background and a flat pedestal of about 1600 counts. The hBN line is only about 250 counts above it (SNR about 12 against local noise of about 20 counts), so its fitted height and area carry a baseline systematic of order 10–20 %.
The 1474 cm-1 feature, the broad 608 cm-1 background hump in the flake 2 fit, and the other small residual structure were not treated as sample bands.
No shift test for heating was possible with one power. Heating softens E2g (1367.7 cm-1 at 75 C, 1366.4 at 100 C, Cai 2017 p.7) so it cannot explain an upshift, and hBN absorbs little at 514.5 nm.

Both spectra were taken at one laser and one polarisation setting. E2g gives no in-plane angular contrast in backscattering by symmetry (inferred, not from a source I read), so polarisation would not help.
questions_for_user: Do you have AFM or step-height data for flake 2 (and flake 1)? One thickness measurement turns this from 'thin' into a layer count and calibrates the intensity ladder.
What is the thickness of flake 1, from AFM or optical contrast? Without it the 10x intensity ratio cannot be turned into N.
Were both spectra taken at the same focus, objective and spot? The Si 520 line differs 18x between them, and that may change the intensity comparison.
Has either flake been annealed, or was it transferred (PDMS, polymer)? Annealing upshifts thin-hBN E2g by about 2–3 cm-1 on SiO2/Si (Cai 2017 Fig. 4), which would mimic the 1L signature.
What is the bulk source and isotope composition (natural B, HPHT, flux-grown)? The width floor differs by a factor of about 2 between natural and enriched crystals.
What are the laser power, objective NA and spectral resolution? Power above a few hundred microwatts risks heating, and a resolution comparable to about 8 cm-1 would hide width differences.
Is a low-frequency range available? The interlayer shear E2g near 50 cm-1 in bulk is absent in a monolayer and would give an independent layer test, but our data start at 450 cm-1.

limits: Raman alone cannot assign N=1 for hBN. No relation in the skill's relation list covers hBN layer number, so the layer assessment comes from the literature notes and the flake-to-flake comparison, not from a validated relation.
I could not calibrate the E2g intensity per layer on 290 nm SiO2 at 514.5 nm. That needs a ladder of AFM-verified flakes, and the Gorbachev data are for a different oxide thickness.

Rejected hypotheses: 2TO Si bands as hBN modes (they are Si); the 1474 cm-1 feature as a real band (noise); carbon contamination near 1350/1580 (no G band, and the 1369 line is narrower and positioned like hBN); heating (it would downshift, not upshift).

Not testable here: crystal quality or defect density (no sourced hBN defect metric), isotope content (width is ambiguous between sources), strain magnitude and sign (no calibrated coefficient), and stacking or twist (only E2g is visible and the shear mode is outside the window).
The dataset starts at 450 cm-1, so the interlayer shear mode (absent for 1L, present near 50 cm-1 in bulk) was not observed; its absence in these data is not evidence.
